{{smaller block|''Attrition'' by virtue of the keys is made contrition.
{{right|Quoted in ''Abp. Ussher’s'' Ans. to a Jesuit, v.}}}}

'''attrition-mill''' (a-trish′ọn-mil), ''n.'' A mill, usually centrifugal, in which grain is pulverized by the mutual attrition of its particles, and by frictional contact with the sides.

'''attritus''' (a-trī′tus), ''n.'' [L., a rubbing on, an inflammation caused by rubbing, < ''attritus'', pp. of ''atterere:'' see ''attrite''. For the sense here given, cf. ''detritus''.] Matter reduced to powder by attrition. ''Carlyle.''

'''attry†''', ''a.'' See ''attery''.

'''attune''' (a̤-tūn′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''attuned'', ppr. ''attuning''. [< ''at-''<sup>2</sup> + ''tune'', q. v.] '''1.''' To tune or put in tune; adjust to harmony of sound; make accordant: as, to ''attune'' the voice to a harp.
{{smaller block|And tongues, ''attuned'' to curses, roar’d applause.
{{right|''Crabbe'', The Borough.}}}}
'''2.''' Figuratively, to arrange fitly; make accordant; bring into harmony: as, to ''attune'' our aims to the divine will.
{{smaller block|The landscape around . . . was one to ''attune'' their souls to holy musings. {{right|''Longfellow'', Hyperion, iv. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|Though my ear was ''attuned'', the songster was tardy.
{{right|''The Century'', XXVII. 776.}}}}
'''3.''' To make musical. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Vernal airs,
Breathing the smell of field and grove, ''attune''
The trembling leaves.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iv. 265.}}}}

'''attune''' (a̤-tūn′), ''n.'' [< ''attune'', ''v.''] Harmony of sounds; accord. ''Mrs. Browning.''

'''attunement''' (a̤-tūn′ment), ''n.'' [< ''attune'' + ''-ment''.] The act of attuning. [Rare.]

¶
'''atturn†''', ''v.'' An obsolete spelling of ''attorn''.

'''atturney†''', ''n.'' An obsolete spelling of ''attorney''.

'''Attus''' (at′us), ''n.'' [NL.; cf. ''Atta''.] '''1.''' A genus of spiders, typical of the family ''Attidæ''.—'''2.''' A genus of hemipterous insects.

'''attypic, attypical''' (a-tip′ik, -i-kạl), ''a.'' [< ''at-''<sup>2</sup> + ''typic'', ''-al''.] In ''zoöl.'', of the particular character acquired, or in process of acquisition, by specialization, from a more generalized type, as from a prototype or archetype: opposed to ''etypical''.
{{smaller block|''Attypical'' characters are those to the acquisition of which, as a matter of fact, we find that forms, in their journey to a specialized condition, tend.
{{right|''Gill'', Proc. Amer. Assoc. Adv. Sci., XX. 293.}}}}

'''attypically''' (a-tip′i-kạl-i), ''adv.'' In an attypic manner.

'''atumble''' (ạ-tum′bl), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''tumble''.] In a tumbling condition.

'''-atus<sup>1</sup>.''' [L. ''-ātus'', fem. ''-āta'', neut. ''-ātum'': see ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.] A Latin termination, the original of ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>, ''-ate''<sup>2</sup>, ''-ade''<sup>1</sup>, ''-ee''<sup>1</sup>, etc., the suffix of perfect participles of the Latin first conjugation, and of adjectives similarly formed. It occurs frequently in New Latin specific names in botany, zoölogy, etc.

'''-atus<sup>2</sup>.''' [L. ''-atus'' (''-atu-''), in nouns of the 4th declension, < ''-āt-'', pp. stem (see ''-atus''<sup>1</sup>), + stem vowel ''-u-''. The Eng. form of this suffix is ''-ate'': see ''-ate''<sup>3</sup>.] A termination of Latin nouns, many of which have been adopted unaltered in English, as ''apparatus'', ''afflatus'', ''flatus'', etc. {{smaller|Such nouns, if they have a plural, retain the Latin form (L. ''-ātūs''), as ''apparatus'', or, rarely, take an English plural, as}}
readings.c1s3:
apparatuses.''

'''atwain†''' (ạ-twān′), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''atwayne'', ''a-tweyne''; < ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''twain''. Cf. ''atwin'' and ''atwo''.] In twain; asunder.
{{smaller block|<poem>A fickle maid full pale,
Tearing of papers, breaking rings ''a-twain'',
Storming her world with sorrow’s wind and rain.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lover’s Complaint, l. 6.}}}}

'''atweel''' (at-wēl′). [Sc., appar. contr. from ''I wat weel'', I know well: ''wat'' = E. ''wot''; ''weel'' = E. ''well''.] I wot well. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|''Atweel'' I would fain tell him. {{right|''Scott'', Antiquary, xxxix.}}}}

'''atween''' (ạ-twēn′), ''prep.'' and ''adv.'' [< ME. ''atweene'', ''atwene''; < ''a-'' + ''-tween'', equiv. to ''between'', q. v.] Between; in or into an intervening space. [Old English and Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>But he, right well aware, his rage to ward
Did cast his shield ''atweene''.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. xii. 30.}}}}

'''atwin†''', ''adv.'' [ME., also ''atwinne''; < ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''twin''. Cf. ''atwain''.] Apart; asunder.
{{smaller block|Thy wif and thou most hangen fer ''a-twinne''.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Miller’s Tale, l. 403.}}}}

'''atwirl''' (ạ-twėrl′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.'' [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''twirl''.] In a twirl; twirling.
{{smaller block|<poem>Goody Cole
Sat by her door with her wheel ''atwirl''.</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', The Wreck of Rivermouth.}}}}

'''atwist''' (ạ-twist′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.'' [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''twist'', ''n.''] Awry; distorted; tangled. [Rare.]

'''atwite†''', ''v. t.'' [Early mod. E. also ''attwite'', < ME. ''atwiten'', < AS. ''ætwītan'', < ''æt'', at, + ''wītan'', blame;
readings.c2s1:
see ''wite''. Hence by apheresis mod. E. ''twit''.] To blame; reproach; twit.

¶
'''atwitter''' (a-twit′ėr), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.'' [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''twitter''.] In a twitter.

'''atwix†''', '''atwixen†''', '''atwixt†''', ''prep.'' [ME. ''atwix'', ''atwixen'', ''atwixe'', ''atwixt'', etc.; < ''a-'' + ''-twixen'', ''twixt''; equiv. to ''betwixen'', ''betwixt'', q. v.] Betwixt; between.
{{smaller block|''Atwixen'' sonne and see.{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, v. 886.}}}}

'''atwo†''', ''adv.'' [ME., < AS. ''on twā'', ''on tū'': see ''a''<sup>3</sup> and ''two''.] In two.
{{smaller block|An axe to smite the cord ''atwo''.{{right|''Chaucer'', Miller’s Tale, l. 383.}}}}

'''Atwood’s machine.''' See ''machine''.
readings.c2s2:
¶
'''atypic''' (a-tip′ik), ''a.'' [< Gr. ἄτυπος, conforming to no distinct type (of illness) (< ἀ- priv. + τύπος, type), + ''-ic'': see ''a-''<sup>18</sup> and ''typic''.] '''1.''' Having no distinct typical character; not typical; not conformable to the type.—'''2.''' Producing a loss of typical characters. ''Dana.''
[[FIGURE]]
{{c|{{smaller|''Atypus sulzeri.'' (Vertical line shows natural size.)}}}}

'''atypical''' (a-tip′i-ka̤l), ''a.'' [< ''atypic'' + ''-al.''] Same as ''atypic.''

'''atypically''' (a-tip′i-ka̤l-i), ''adv.'' In an atypic manner.

'''Atypinæ''' (at-i-pī′nē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Atypus'', 1, + ''-inæ.''] A subfamily of ''Theraphosidæ'' or ''Mygalidæ'' distinguished by the development of six spinners, typified by the genus ''Atypus.''

'''Atypus''' (at′i-pus), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. ἄτυπος, conforming to no distinct type, < ἀ- priv. + τύπος, type: see ''type.''] '''1.''' A genus of spiders, of the family ''Theraphosidæ'' or ''Mygalidæ'', having six arachnidial mammillæ or spinnerets. {{smaller|''A. piceus'' is a European species which digs a hole in the ground and lines it with silk. The genus with some authors gives name to a subfamily ''Atypinæ.''}}

'''2.''' A genus of fishes, now called ''Atypichthys.'' ''Günther'', 1860.
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''au'''<sup>1</sup>. [< ME. ''au'', ''aw'', or ''a'' before a guttural, nasal, or ''l'' (''aȝ'', ''ah'', ''al'' (''aul''), etc.), of AS. or OF. or L. origin.] A common English digraph representing generally the sound of “broad a” (â), but often also ä. {{smaller|It occurs only exceptionally, and by conformation with Romanic analogies, in words of Anglo-Saxon origin, as in ''aught'', ''taught'', ''daughter'', ''haulm''=''halm'', ''baulk''=''balk'' (and formerly as a variant, medially, with ''aw'', as in ''baul'', ''hauk'', etc., for ''bawl'', ''hawk'', etc.). In words of Old French (and ultimately Latin) origin it represents an original ''al'', now sometimes ''aul'' as in ''fault'', ''assault'', etc., or ''a'' before a nasal, as in ''aunt'', ''haunch'', ''launch'', etc. (but in most such words now usually simplified to ''a'', as in ''grand'', ''grant'', ''lance'', etc.). It is frequently of Latin origin, as in ''audit'', ''cause'', ''laud'', etc., or of Greek origin, as in ''caustic''. In words from recent French it may have the present F. sound (ō) as in ''hauteur'', ''au fait'', etc. In words of German and usually of other foreign origin, it has its analytical value (ä + u), corresponding to English ''ou'' in ''sour'', as in ''sauerkraut'', ''ablaut'', ''umlaut''. Formerly ''au'' and ''aw'' were used almost indifferently; but now ''au'' is never final in English words, while ''aw'' is rarely medial, except in a few familiar words, as in ''hawk'', ''bawl'', but regularly final, as in ''law'', ''saw'', ''claw'', etc. See ''aw''.}}

'''au'''<sup>2</sup> (ō). [F., < OF. ''au'', ''o'', ''ou'', earlier ''al'', contr. of ''a le'' = Sp. Pg. ''al'' = It. ''all'', ''allo'', < L. ''ad illum'' (m.) or ''ad illud'' (neut.): ''ad'', to, with acc. of ''ille'', that, in Rom. the def. art. ‘the.’ The corresp. fem. is ''à la'', q. v.] To the; at the; with the: the dative of the French definite article, occurring in some phrases frequently used in English, as ''au fait'', ''au fond'', ''au revoir'', etc.

'''Au.''' The chemical symbol of gold (L., ''aurum'').

'''aubade''' (ō-bȧd′), ''n.'' [F., < ''aube'', dawn (< L. ''alba'', fem. of ''albus'', white; cf. ''aube'' = ''alb''<sup>1</sup>), after Sp. ''albada'', aubade, < ''alba'', dawn: see ''alb''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' In
readings.c2s4:
troubadour and similar music, a song or piece to be performed in the open air in the early morning, usually addressed to some special person; a musical announcement of dawn. See ''serenade''.
{{smaller block|<poem>There he lingered till the crowing cock,
The Alectryon of the farmyard and the flock,
Sang his ''aubade'' with lusty voice and clear.</poem>
{{right|''Longfellow'', Wayside Inn, Emma and Eginhard.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''modern music'', a rarely used title for a short instrumental composition in lyric style.

'''aubain''' (ō-bān′; F. pron. ō-baṅ′), ''n.'' [F., < ML. ''albanus'', an alien, < L. ''alibi'', elsewhere, + ''-anus'': see ''alibi''.] A non-naturalized foreigner, subject to the right of aubaine. ''N. E. D.''

'''aubaine''' (ō-bān′), ''n.'' [F., < ''aubain'': see ''aubain''.] Succession to the goods of a stranger not naturalized. {{smaller|The ''droit d’aubaine'' in France was a right of the king to the goods of an alien dying within his realm,}}
readings.c3s1:
{{smaller block|the king standing in the place of the heirs. This right was abolished in 1819.}}

¶
'''aube†''', ''n.'' [F., < L. ''alba'', alb: see ''alb''<sup>1</sup>.] Obsolete form of ''alb''<sup>1</sup>. ''Fuller.''

'''auberge''' (â′bėrj; F. pron. ō-bārzh′), ''n.'' [F., < OF. ''alberge'' (= Pr. ''alberc'' = Sp. ''albergue'' = It. ''albergo'', an inn), earlier ''helberge'', orig. ''herberge'', a military station, < MHG. ''herberge'', OHG. ''heriberga'', a camp, lodging, G. ''herberge'', an inn: see ''harbinger'' and ''harbor''<sup>1</sup>.] An inn. ''Beau. and Fl.''

'''aubergine''' (â′bėr-jin; F. pron. ō-bār-zhēn′), ''n.'' [F., dim. of ''auberge'', ''alberge'', a kind of peach, < Sp. ''albérchigo'', ''albérchiga'' (= Pg. ''alperche''), a peach, < Ar. ''al'', the, + Sp. ''pérsigo'', ''prisco'' = Pg. ''pecego'' = F. ''pêche'' (> E. ''peach''<sup>1</sup>), < L. ''persicum'': see ''peach''<sup>1</sup>. The Sp. forms touch those of ''apricot'': see ''apricot''.] The fruit of the egg-plant, ''Solanum Melongena''; the brinjal.

'''aubergist, aubergiste''' (â′bėr-jist; F. pron. ō-bār-zhēst′), ''n.'' [< F. ''aubergiste'', inn-keeper, < ''auberge'': see ''auberge''.] The keeper of an auberge; an inn-keeper; a tavern-keeper; a landlord or landlady: as, “the ''aubergiste'' at Terni,” ''Smollett.''

'''aubin''' (ō-baṅ′), ''n.'' [F., < OF. ''haubin'', ''hobin'', an ambling nag: see ''hobby''.] In the ''manège'', a kind of broken gait, between an amble and a gallop, commonly called a “Canterbury gallop,” and accounted a defect.

'''auburn''' (â′bėrn), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [Early mod. E. ''auborn'', ''abourne'' (also ''abrown'', ''abroun'', ''abrune'', simulating ''brown''), < ME. ''auburne'', ''awburne'' (defined “''citrinus'',” i. e., citron-colored, in Prompt. Parv.), < OF. ''auborne'', ''alborne'' = It. ''alburno'', auburn, < ML. ''alburnus'', whitish, < L. ''albus'',
readings.c3s2:
white. Cf. ''alburn'', ''alburnum''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Originally, whitish or flaxen-colored; now, reddish-brown: generally applied to hair.
{{smaller block|That whitish colour of a woman’s hair called an ''aburn'' colour.
{{right|''Florio.''}}}}
'''II.''' ''n.'' An auburn color.
{{smaller block|<poem>He’s white-haired,
Not wanton white, but such a manly colour,
Next to an ''auburn.''</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''), Two Noble Kinsmen, iv. 2.}}}}

'''A. U. C.''' Abbreviation of Latin ''ab urbe condita'' or ''anno urbis conditæ'' (which see).

'''Auchenia''' (â-kē′ni-ä), ''n.'' [NL. (Illiger, 1811), < Gr. αὐχήν, neck: in allusion to the long neck of the llama.] A genus of ruminants, of the family ''Camelidæ'', representing in the new world the camels of the old, but having no hump. {{smaller|The genus includes four important and well-known quadrupeds indigenous to South America, namely, the llama (''A. llama''), the guanaco (''A. huanaco''), the alpaca (''A. pacos''), and the vicugna (''A. vicugna''). The second of these is by some supposed to be the wild stock of the llama, which is now known only in domestication. See cuts under ''alpaca'', ''guanaco'', ''llama'', and ''vicugna''.}}

'''auchenium''' (â-kē′ni-um), ''n.''; pl. ''auchenia'' (-ạ̈). [NL., < Gr. αὐχήν, neck.] In ''ornith.'', the lower back part of the neck; the scruff of the neck, just below the nape. ''Illiger''; ''Sundevall.'' [Little used.]

'''Auchenorhynchi''' (â-kē-nọ̄-ring′kī), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < Gr. αὐχήν, neck, + ῥύγχος, snout.] A group of hemipterous insects: synonymous with ''Homoptera''.
readings.c3s3:
¶
'''auchlet''' (âċh′let), ''n.'' [Sc., < ''aucht'', = E. ''eight'', + ''lot'', part. Cf. ''firlot''.] In Scotland, a measure equal to the eighth part of a boll.

'''aucht<sup>1</sup>''' (âċht), ''v.'' Same as ''aught''<sup>2</sup>. [Scotch.]

'''aucht<sup>2</sup>''' (äċht), ''a.'' and ''n.'' Same as ''aught''<sup>4</sup>. [Scotch.]

'''au courant''' (ō kö-roṅ′). [F.: ''au'', with the (see ''au''<sup>2</sup>); ''courant'', current (see ''courant'', ''current'').] Literally, in the current, that is, of events; well informed in regard to any event or subject.

'''auctificial†''', ''a.'' Same as ''auctive''. ''Coles.''

'''auction''' (âk′shọn), ''n.'' [< L. ''auctio''(''n''-), an increasing, a sale by auction, < ''augere'', pp. ''auctus'', increase, = E. ''eke'', ''v.'', q. v.] '''1†.''' The act of increasing; increase; growth. ''Bailey.''—'''2.''' A public sale in which each bidder offers an increase on the previous bid, the highest bidder becoming the purchaser. {{smaller|Called in Scotland a ''roup''. Goods may be said to be sold either ''at'' or ''by'' auction, the former use prevailing in the United States and the latter in Great Britain.}}
{{smaller block|The old books would have been worth nothing at an ''auction''.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Old Manse, I.}}}}
'''3†.''' The property or goods put up for sale at auction.
{{smaller block|<poem>Ask you why Phryne the whole ''auction'' buys?
Phryne foresees a general excise.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Moral Essays, iii. 119.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Auction by inch of candle''', an old method of selling by auction, still sometimes practised, in which a small piece of candle is lighted at the beginning of a sale, and the highest bid made before the wick falls is successful.—'''Dutch auction.''' See ''Dutch''.}}

'''atwitter''' (a-twit′ėr), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.''   [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''twitter''.]   In a twitter.

'''atwix†''', '''atwixen†''', '''atwixt†''', ''prep.''   [ME. ''atwix'', ''atwixen'', ''atwixe'', ''atwixt'', etc.; < ''a-'' + ''-twixen'', ''twixt''; equiv. to ''betwixen'', ''betwixt'', q. v.]   Betwixt; between.
{{smaller block|''Atwixen'' sonne and see.{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, v. 886.}}}}

'''atwo†''', ''adv.''   [ME., < AS. ''on twā'', ''on tū'': see ''a''<sup>3</sup> and ''two''.]   In two.
{{smaller block|An axe to smite the cord ''atwo''.{{right|''Chaucer'', Miller’s Tale, l. 383.}}}}

'''Atwood’s machine.''' See ''machine''.

'''atypic''' (a-tip′ik), ''a.''   [< Gr. ἄτυπος, conforming to no distinct type (of illness) (< ἀ- priv. + τύπος, type), + ''-ic'': see ''a-''<sup>18</sup> and ''typic''.]   '''1.''' Having no distinct typical character; not typical; not conformable to the type.—'''2.''' Producing a loss of typical characters.   ''Dana.'' {{img float|file=century v01 p0402 c2f1.png|width=147px|align=right|cap={{smaller|''Atypus sulzeri.'' (Vertical line shows natural size.)}}}}

'''atypical''' (a-tip′i-ka̤l), ''a.''   [< ''atypic'' + ''-al.'']   Same as ''atypic.''

'''atypically''' (a-tip′i-ka̤l-i), ''adv.'' In an atypic manner.

'''Atypinæ''' (at-i-pī′nē), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Atypus'', 1, + ''-inæ.'']   A subfamily of ''Theraphosidæ'' or ''Mygalidæ'' distinguished by the development of six spinners, typified by the genus ''Atypus.''

'''Atypus''' (at′i-pus), ''n.''   [NL., < Gr. ἄτυπος, conforming to no distinct type, < ἀ- priv. + τύπος, type: see ''type.'']   '''1.''' A genus of spiders, of the family ''Theraphosidæ'' or ''Mygalidæ'', having six arachnidial mammillæ or spinnerets. {{smaller|''A. piceus'' is a European species which digs a hole in the ground and lines it with silk. The genus with some authors gives name to a subfamily ''Atypinæ.''}}

'''2.''' A genus of fishes, now called ''Atypichthys.''   ''Günther'', 1860.

'''au'''<sup>1</sup>.   [< ME. ''au'', ''aw'', or ''a'' before a guttural, nasal, or ''l'' (''aȝ'', ''ah'', ''al'' (''aul''), etc.), of AS. or OF. or L. origin.]   A common English digraph representing generally the sound of “broad a” (â), but often also ä. {{smaller|It occurs only exceptionally, and by conformation with Romanic analogies, in words of Anglo-Saxon origin, as in ''aught'', ''taught'', ''daughter'', ''haulm''=''halm'', ''baulk''=''balk'' (and formerly as a variant, medially, with ''aw'', as in ''baul'', ''hauk'', etc., for ''bawl'', ''hawk'', etc.). In words of Old French (and ultimately Latin) origin it represents an original ''al'', now sometimes ''aul'' as in ''fault'', ''assault'', etc., or ''a'' before a nasal, as in ''aunt'', ''haunch'', ''launch'', etc. (but in most such words now usually simplified to ''a'', as in ''grand'', ''grant'', ''lance'', etc.). It is frequently of Latin origin, as in ''audit'', ''cause'', ''laud'', etc., or of Greek origin, as in ''caustic''. In words from recent French it may have the present F. sound (ō) as in ''hauteur'', ''au fait'', etc. In words of German and usually of other foreign origin, it has its analytical value (ä + u), corresponding to English ''ou'' in ''sour'', as in ''sauerkraut'', ''ablaut'', ''umlaut''. Formerly ''au'' and ''aw'' were used almost indifferently; but now ''au'' is never final in English words, while ''aw'' is rarely medial, except in a few familiar words, as in ''hawk'', ''bawl'', but regularly final, as in ''law'', ''saw'', ''claw'', etc. See ''aw''.}}

'''au'''<sup>2</sup> (ō).   [F., < OF. ''au'', ''o'', ''ou'', earlier ''al'', contr. of ''a le'' = Sp. Pg. ''al'' = It. ''all'', ''allo'', < L. ''ad illum'' (m.) or ''ad illud'' (neut.): ''ad'', to, with acc. of ''ille'', that, in Rom. the def. art. ‘the.’ The corresp. fem. is ''à la'', q. v.]   To the; at the; with the: the dative of the French definite article, occurring in some phrases frequently used in English, as ''au fait'', ''au fond'', ''au revoir'', etc.

'''Au.''' The chemical symbol of gold (L., ''aurum'').

'''aubade''' (ō-bȧd′), ''n.''   [F., < ''aube'', dawn (< L. ''alba'', fem. of ''albus'', white; cf. ''aube'' = ''alb''<sup>1</sup>), after Sp. ''albada'', aubade, < ''alba'', dawn: see ''alb''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' In troubadour and similar music, a song or piece to be performed in the open air in the early morning, usually addressed to some special person; a musical announcement of dawn. See ''serenade''.
{{smaller block|<poem>There he lingered till the crowing cock,
The Alectryon of the farmyard and the flock,
Sang his ''aubade'' with lusty voice and clear.</poem>
{{right|''Longfellow'', Wayside Inn, Emma and Eginhard.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''modern music'', a rarely used title for a short instrumental composition in lyric style.

'''aubain''' (ō-bān′; F. pron. ō-baṅ′), ''n.''   [F., < ML. ''albanus'', an alien, < L. ''alibi'', elsewhere, + ''-anus'': see ''alibi''.]   A non-naturalized foreigner, subject to the right of aubaine.   ''N. E. D.''

'''aubaine''' (ō-bān′), ''n.''   [F., < ''aubain'': see ''aubain''.]   Succession to the goods of a stranger not naturalized. {{smaller|The ''droit d’aubaine'' in France was a right of the king to the goods of an alien dying within his realm, the king standing in the place of the heirs. This right was abolished in 1819.}}

'''aube†''', ''n.''   [F., < L. ''alba'', alb: see ''alb''<sup>1</sup>.]   Obsolete form of ''alb''<sup>1</sup>.   ''Fuller.''

'''auberge''' (â′bėrj; F. pron. ō-bārzh′), ''n.''   [F., < OF. ''alberge'' (= Pr. ''alberc'' = Sp. ''albergue'' = It. ''albergo'', an inn), earlier ''helberge'', orig. ''herberge'', a military station, < MHG. ''herberge'', OHG. ''heriberga'', a camp, lodging, G. ''herberge'', an inn: see ''harbinger'' and ''harbor''<sup>1</sup>.]   An inn.   ''Beau. and Fl.''

'''aubergine''' (â′bėr-jin; F. pron. ō-bār-zhēn′), ''n.''   [F., dim. of ''auberge'', ''alberge'', a kind of peach, < Sp. ''albérchigo'', ''albérchiga'' (= Pg. ''alperche''), a peach, < Ar. ''al'', the, + Sp. ''pérsigo'', ''prisco'' = Pg. ''pecego'' = F. ''pêche'' (> E. ''peach''<sup>1</sup>), < L. ''persicum'': see ''peach''<sup>1</sup>. The Sp. forms touch those of ''apricot'': see ''apricot''.]   The fruit of the egg-plant, ''Solanum Melongena''; the brinjal.

'''aubergist, aubergiste''' (â′bėr-jist; F. pron. ō-bār-zhēst′), ''n.''   [< F. ''aubergiste'', inn-keeper, < ''auberge'': see ''auberge''.]   The keeper of an auberge; an inn-keeper; a tavern-keeper; a landlord or landlady: as, “the ''aubergiste'' at Terni,” ''Smollett.''

'''aubin''' (ō-baṅ′), ''n.''   [F., < OF. ''haubin'', ''hobin'', an ambling nag: see ''hobby''.]   In the ''manège'', a kind of broken gait, between an amble and a gallop, commonly called a “Canterbury gallop,” and accounted a defect.

'''auburn''' (â′bėrn), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [Early mod. E. ''auborn'', ''abourne'' (also ''abrown'', ''abroun'', ''abrune'', simulating ''brown''), < ME. ''auburne'', ''awburne'' (defined “''citrinus'',” i. e., citron-colored, in Prompt. Parv.), < OF. ''auborne'', ''alborne'' = It. ''alburno'', auburn, < ML. ''alburnus'', whitish, < L. ''albus'', white. Cf. ''alburn'', ''alburnum''.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' Originally, whitish or flaxen-colored; now, reddish-brown: generally applied to hair.
{{smaller block|That whitish colour of a woman’s hair called an ''aburn'' colour.
{{right|''Florio.''}}}}
'''II.''' ''n.'' An auburn color.
{{smaller block|<poem>He’s white-haired,
Not wanton white, but such a manly colour,
Next to an ''auburn.''</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''), Two Noble Kinsmen, iv. 2.}}}}

'''A. U. C.''' Abbreviation of Latin ''ab urbe condita'' or ''anno urbis conditæ'' (which see).

'''Auchenia''' (â-kē′ni-ä), ''n.''   [NL. (Illiger, 1811), < Gr. αὐχήν, neck: in allusion to the long neck of the llama.]   A genus of ruminants, of the family ''Camelidæ'', representing in the new world the camels of the old, but having no hump. {{smaller|The genus includes four important and well-known quadrupeds indigenous to South America, namely, the llama (''A. llama''), the guanaco (''A. huanaco''), the alpaca (''A. pacos''), and the vicugna (''A. vicugna''). The second of these is by some supposed to be the wild stock of the llama, which is now known only in domestication. See cuts under ''alpaca'', ''guanaco'', ''llama'', and ''vicugna''.}}

'''auchenium''' (â-kē′ni-um), ''n.''; pl. ''auchenia'' (-ạ̈).   [NL., < Gr. αὐχήν, neck.]   In ''ornith.'', the lower back part of the neck; the scruff of the neck, just below the nape. ''Illiger'';   ''Sundevall.'' [Little used.]

'''Auchenorhynchi''' (â-kē-nọ̄-ring′kī), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < Gr. αὐχήν, neck, + ῥύγχος, snout.]   A group of hemipterous insects: synonymous with ''Homoptera''.

'''auchlet''' (âċh′let), ''n.''   [Sc., < ''aucht'', = E. ''eight'', + ''lot'', part. Cf. ''firlot''.]   In Scotland, a measure equal to the eighth part of a boll.

'''aucht<sup>1</sup>''' (âċht), ''v.'' Same as ''aught''<sup>2</sup>.   [Scotch.]

'''aucht<sup>2</sup>''' (äċht), ''a.'' and ''n.'' Same as ''aught''<sup>4</sup>.   [Scotch.]

'''au courant''' (ō kö-roṅ′).   [F.: ''au'', with the (see ''au''<sup>2</sup>); ''courant'', current (see ''courant'', ''current'').]   Literally, in the current, that is, of events; well informed in regard to any event or subject.

'''auctificial†''', ''a.'' Same as ''auctive''.   ''Coles.''

'''auction''' (âk′shọn), ''n.''   [< L. ''auctio''(''n''-), an increasing, a sale by auction, < ''augere'', pp. ''auctus'', increase, = E. ''eke'', ''v.'', q. v.]   '''1†.''' The act of increasing; increase; growth.   ''Bailey.''—'''2.''' A public sale in which each bidder offers an increase on the previous bid, the highest bidder becoming the purchaser. {{smaller|Called in Scotland a ''roup''. Goods may be said to be sold either ''at'' or ''by'' auction, the former use prevailing in the United States and the latter in Great Britain.}}
{{smaller block|The old books would have been worth nothing at an ''auction''.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Old Manse, I.}}}}
'''3†.''' The property or goods put up for sale at auction.
{{smaller block|<poem>Ask you why Phryne the whole ''auction'' buys?
Phryne foresees a general excise.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Moral Essays, iii. 119.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Auction by inch of candle''', an old method of selling by auction, still sometimes practised, in which a small piece of candle is lighted at the beginning of a sale, and the highest bid made before the wick falls is successful.—'''Dutch auction.''' See ''Dutch''.}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
